opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually a really interesting signal, because a lot of people expected the opposite. The naive story was: AI writes code now, so you need fewer engineers. But what I think is happening is closer to a Jevons paradox type of thing. When you make something dramatically cheaper and easier to produce, demand for it doesn't shrink, it explodes. Software has always been bottlenecked by how expensive it is to write and maintain. Every company has this enormous backlog of things they'd love to build but never could justify. As the cost per unit of software comes down, all of that latent demand starts to become economically viable.

The other part is that the job itself is shifting. I don't think "engineer" means quite the same thing it did a few years ago. You're spending less time typing out every line and more time specifying, reviewing, directing these models, and catching where they go off the rails. They're incredibly capable in some ways and surprisingly dumb in others, so you need someone in the loop who actually understands the system, has taste, and can tell when something is subtly wrong. That person becomes more leveraged, not less. One good engineer can now do what used to take a small team, and companies are realizing that's a great deal, so they want more of them.

I'd also say we're still very early. A lot of the infrastructure, the tooling, the way organizations integrate this stuff, it's all being built right now, and building it takes a lot of engineering. So in the near term, I think it makes total sense that demand keeps rising. Longer term, the nature of the work will keep changing, and people will have to keep adapting. But I'm pretty optimistic. I think more people are going to be building software than ever before, not fewer.

r001.rationale: The response says software has been bottlenecked by the cost of writing and maintaining it, leaving a backlog of desired projects unjustifiable until costs fall. This clearly suggests software scarcity constrains demand.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's actually really interesting, because there was this narrative, maybe a year or two ago, that software engineering was going to be one of the first things to go. And what we're seeing is kind of the opposite, at least so far. I think there are a few things going on.

The first is that these tools are not autonomous engineers yet. They're more like a very fast, very knowledgeable intern who sometimes makes stuff up. So you still need a person in the loop who understands the system, who can read the code, who can tell when the model is confidently wrong. And that person is an engineer. If anything the job shifts toward judgment and verification rather than typing, but the demand for the judgment goes up, not down.

The second thing is just Jevons paradox, basically. When you make something cheaper, people consume a lot more of it. Software was expensive to produce, so a huge amount of software that "should" exist just never got built, because the economics didn't work. Now the cost of a line of code is dropping, and suddenly a lot of those projects become viable. So you get more software, more systems, more things that need to be maintained and integrated, and all of that still needs people.

And the third thing, which I think people underweight, is that the AI stuff itself is an enormous engineering surface. Training infrastructure, data pipelines, evals, deployment, agent harnesses, all of this is very much unsolved and very much hands-on engineering work. So the technology that was supposed to replace engineers is itself generating a lot of engineering demand.

I'd put one caveat on it though. I think the kind of engineer being demanded is changing. The person who is good at this new world is less of a "I know the syntax of this language really well" person and more of a "I can decompose the problem, I can supervise the model, I can tell good from bad output" person. So the headline number going up hides a fairly significant shift in what the job actually is.

r001.rationale: The response says software was expensive to produce, so many projects that should exist were never built because the economics did not work. This communicates that limited availability constrained software demand.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether we’re talking about demand for writing code or demand for building software. Those are different things. You can automate more of the code writing and still have a huge amount of demand for people who can figure out what to build, make it work, and take responsibility for the result.

If software becomes much cheaper to produce, suddenly a lot of projects that weren’t worth doing become worth doing. Every company has this backlog of things they would love to automate or improve. So you could have engineers becoming dramatically more productive and, at the same time, more demand for engineering.

The job changes, though. You spend less time typing out the implementation and more time specifying what you want, checking what the AI did, and making sure all the pieces actually fit together. I don’t think increasing demand is necessarily evidence that AI isn’t having an impact. It could also be a consequence of software becoming more accessible and useful.

r001.rationale: The response says making software cheaper to produce would make previously uneconomical projects worthwhile, communicating that limited, costly software production constrains realized demand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one way to interpret it is that demand for software is much larger than the amount we can currently produce. So when you make engineers more productive, it doesn’t necessarily mean you need fewer engineers. It can mean that a whole bunch of projects that weren’t worth doing before suddenly become worth doing.

And engineering is not just typing code. It’s figuring out what to build, understanding the constraints, and checking that the thing actually works. AI can help a lot with implementation, but someone still has to direct that process and take responsibility for the result.

So I don’t think increasing demand is inconsistent with increasingly capable AI. The work can change quite dramatically while the amount of work people want done continues to grow.

r001.rationale: The response says demand for software exceeds what can currently be produced and that increased productivity makes previously unworthwhile projects viable, conveying that limited software production constrains demand.
